subject: dwarfBlacksmith
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: dwarf blacksmith at an anvil.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a dwarf blacksmith character at an anvil in a Warcraft-style aesthetic—chunky proportions, big shoulders and hands, braided beard, heavy pauldrons, apron, hammer, and a glowing hot blade on the anvil, while thinking through how to structure the module's code carefully since I can't test it directly.

I'm working out the skeleton and pose: hips as root at roughly hip height, spine chain up through neck and head, with the right arm holding the hammer and the left arm extending forward to hold tongs with a blade resting on the anvil in front of him, aiming for a readable neutral stance with limbs separated and extended rather than a stiff T-pose.

Now I'm calculating the leg IK, placing hips, knees, and ankles with thigh and shin lengths that keep the stance proportionate and the knees bending forward naturally, then moving on to torso proportions with the pelvis, chest, and shoulder heights sized for a stocky barrel-chested dwarf build.

For the head, I'm sketching a large, bald head with ginger hair and sideburns, goggles pushed up on the forehead with a strap, and keeping the overall design manageable rather than overcomplicating it with extra braids or headwear.

Rather than fighting with joint-local coordinate orientation, I decide to just use absolute model-space coordinates for placing parts, defining a head center point and building spheres and scaled ellipsoids from there for robustness.

For materials, I'm weighing whether to pull in paints from the clockwork and glow kits for metal and glowing effects versus just defining my own paints, since importing kits adds some risk of module resolution issues even though it's allowed.

For textures, I'm planning SVG decals: deep-set brow-shadowed eyes, a root-to-tip gradient beard tuft card, an anvil-and-hammer clan crest on the leather apron, glowing runes on the hammer head and anvil, and a simple emblem for the pauldron.

I also want a heat-gradient glow strip for the blade, studded strap trim for the bracers, an ember spark card, and worn paint on the anvil top — then I'll move into skeleton setup, starting with a root hips joint and building out the spine chain from there.

Still defining skeleton joints...

Adding a jaw joint for the lower jaw/beard parts, then sizing the skull ellipsoid and placing the head top around 1.35-1.4 to fit the dwarf's overall height proportions with goggles included.

Shoulders are wide at ±0.3-0.34 for chunky hands and big pauldrons, with the neck short so the head sits low between them. I'm setting up a torso loft with width/height stations along the spine path, figuring out how the frame's normal and binormal axes map to the body's front/back and side dimensions.

Defining torso loft stations...

I'll define four torso centers forming a slight curve, with a three-segment chain (spine1, spine2, chest) running through them so the chest joint sits near the top, aimed upward, and shoulders/children attach there. I'll add a separate pelvis box for the hips, and plan the torso covering as a tunic with a leather apron and chest strap over it.

For the dwarf's outfit, I'm leaning toward an Ironforge-blue sleeveless tunic with gold trim, a leather apron, and bronze/steel pauldrons with gold trim and rivets -- an asymmetrical blacksmith look with bare muscular arms. I'm placing shoulder joints at ±0.3 on the x-axis at y=1.0, with the right arm set to hold tongs.

Working out the arm kinematics now, calculating joint positions, limb lengths, and target reach distances for the hammer-wielding arm and tong-holding arm so the elbow bends look natural while hammering onto the anvil.

Now I'm placing the anvil itself: positioning its face top, dimensions, and the blade lying across it, with the tongs gripping the tang end while the hand coordinates line up against the anvil's x and z position.

Next I'm figuring out the raised hammer arm, lifting it above the blade at a resting striking position before it comes down.

Computing the handle direction so the hammer head lands high and forward, I check it doesn't collide with the dwarf's face—then reconsider, angling the handle more forward and cocked so the head rests lower for a more natural pose.

For the fist gripping the handle, I'm planning the geometry as a chunky palm box with four rounded finger shapes wrapping around and a separate thumb piece.

Still working out the finger geometry...

I'll treat it as a chunky fist wrapping the handle with a palm box and thumb capsule, then apply the same approach to the left hand gripping tongs using its own handle direction vector, computing hand center as an offset from the wrist target point.

Working through the hammer head geometry...

For the swing-down strike onto the anvil, the head's long axis needs to sit in the vertical plane of the arm's motion, so I'm computing it as the cross product of the handle direction with the x-axis, which gives a vector pointing up and slightly back -- that becomes the orientation for the striking faces.

I'll model the head as a box with a 0.1x0.1 square cross-section along this axis (cross-section symmetry means I don't need to worry about rotation there), add cylindrical faces at the ends for the strike surfaces, use a slightly larger box for the eye/collar bands, and build the handle as a wood-grain rod with a pommel cap, leather wrap near the grip, and a small overhang above the head.

Next I'm designing the tongs as two flattened rods running from the hand to the jaws, pivoting around a rivet point roughly 40% along their length, attached via a bone joint at the hand, with jaw tips gripping the blade. Then I'll shape the glowing sword blade as a tapered extrusion lying on the anvil.

I'll color the blade in bands—white-hot tip, orange mid-section, reddish cooling area, and dark tang near the tongs—building each as a tapered extrude segment using a width function along the blade's length, plus a darker fuller groove line. The blade billet runs roughly from tip at x=-0.3 to the tongs' grip point around x=0.08-0.15.

Now I'm shifting to designing the anvil setup: a log stump with bark texture and steel hoops as the base, topped with a chunky Warcraft-style anvil built from a foot block, a waist taper, and a flat face box.

I'm positioning the horn as a tapering cone extending along x, adding the hardy hole as a dark square cutout on top, and a small heel step at the back end. For materials, I'm giving the body a dark polished iron finish with a thin steel slab on top, plus a glowing orange rune decal on the waist front face.

Now I'm planning the rest of the dwarf's anatomy: chunky boots with steel toe caps and buckle straps, thick leg sweeps tapering from thigh to ankle in dark leather trousers, and a wide belt at the hips to anchor everything together.

I'm also adding a belt with a gold crest buckle, hanging tool loops (hammer, pliers) and a pouch at the right hip, plus a leather apron extruded from chest to knee with a scalloped bottom, positioning it carefully against the torso's front curvature so it sits naturally over the belly without clipping.

Thinking through how to shape the apron itself, I lean toward a loft rather than a flat extrude -- building vertical stations from chest to hip with widths and slight z-offsets following the body's front curve, then deciding whether to rig it to the hips bone so it stays rigid rather than deforming awkwardly with the spine.

I'm settling on binding the apron to the bone chain spanning hips and spine, trusting the path projection to handle joints beyond the chain's ends reasonably.

Weighing an alternative: a flat extruded apron plane wouldn't follow the belly's bulge well, so tilting it or sticking with the loft approach seems better. Leaning toward a loft with a boxy cross-section rather than a thin ellipse, since a circular section would round off the edges too much.

For the apron's appearance, I'm planning leather paint with soot-darkened wear at the bottom, plus a gold-colored anvil-and-hammer clan crest decal placed on the front of the loft geometry.

I'm also sketching neck and shoulder straps draping from the apron's top corners up over the shoulders to the back of the neck, using drape paths against the torso surface, though I realize the shoulder area will mostly be hidden by pauldrons anyway.

Since the torso loft may not fully cover the trapezius region, I'm considering adding a shoulder "yoke" mass as an ellipsoid spanning across the top, then draping straps onto the combined torso-plus-yoke surface, with the belt handled separately via a surface loop around the hips.

For the belt itself, I'm working out the sweep geometry — since it's a horizontal closed loop, the tube's binormal runs sideways while the frame normal points vertically, so the band height should follow the normal direction.

I should use the radius as a function returning the ellipse dimensions rather than a linear taper array, confirming rx is the sideways/binormal direction. For belt placement, I'm lifting the loop slightly outward from the torso surface for a proud look, then figuring out where to position the buckle by raycasting the front of the torso at zero elevation and sticking a box geometry there.

For the buckle itself, I'll orient a thin box along the normal for thickness, skip trying to decal a crest texture onto it since box UV mapping is awkward for small parts, and just go with a gilt frame, steel center, and rivets for a reasonably convincing look. Given the target part count of 180-340 with 5-12 textures, I'm planning to write helper functions and use loops to generate repeated detail elements efficiently.

Setting up the helper functions now...

Now I'm designing the skin material with a paint function that blends ruddy tan base tones using noise for mottling, then darkens toward a shadow tone for added depth and realism near the cheeks.

Next I need to make sure paint callbacks only declare parameters they actually use, since unused ones would fail typechecking. I'm moving on to the leather material for the apron, planning a brown base with noise-driven grain and darker soot shading toward the lower edge.

Beyond that, the tunic underneath needs a deep Ironforge blue with mottled fold noise and a gold trim at the collar, though sleeves aren't necessary since the apron covers most of it. The real focal point is the beard — a massive braided ginger dwarf beard with gold rings, built from hierarchical ellipsoid shapes forming a spade silhouette at the jaw, layered with hair-card textures for volume.

I'm working out the two chest braids as chains of small alternating-tilt ellipsoids placed along a curved path, using frame-based placement so each segment follows the tangent direction with a gold ring band between links for that classic braided look.

Then I'm placing gold torus rings every few segments along the braid and adding a gold cap tassel at the end. I'm attaching the beard and braids to the jaw bone so they move naturally with jaw motion, and sketching the mustache as two thick upward-curling catmull sweeps with gold rings, attached to the head bone. Now I'm starting on the head parts themselves — the skull ellipsoid in skin tone, then moving on to the brow ridge shape.

Placing calculations for ears with small round shapes and gold earring rings, plus ruddy cheek pads positioned symmetrically on the face.

Next I'm figuring out the goggles resting on the forehead—computing the curve of the skull surface to angle the lens cylinders correctly, with brass rims and a teal glow, tilted forward-up and positioned just above the brow line.

I'm positioning the goggle lenses on the strap, checking they sit just above the brows and eyes without overlapping, with the bridge connecting them centered around z 0.225.

For hair, I'm planning a ginger mass behind the goggles and at the sides, forming into sideburns that merge into the beard, plus a short back braid reusing the existing braid function rather than a full ponytail.

For the jaw and mouth, I'll place a small skin ellipsoid for the jaw mostly hidden under the mustache and beard, with a dark mouth-cavity ellipsoid tucked behind the mustache to suggest a mouth gap without needing visible teeth.

I'm working out the skeleton joint chain: a neck joint connecting up to the head, then a jaw joint positioned near the hinge point below the ear, aimed slightly forward and down so the lower jaw parts attach naturally. Now I'm moving on to planning the pauldron armor pieces as layered shoulder guards.

Adding studs, a top spike, and a crest emblem using a lathe profile that traces the dome outline from the axis outward and back, closing into a solid form, with bronze plating as the color choice.

For materials, I'm defining Ironforge-style paint functions: a blue plate with noise-based mottling and edge highlights for a cel-shaded look, plus metal presets for gilt, bronze, steel, and iron. Then I'm sweeping arm geometry along the limb chain with a muscular radius profile, and adding a leather bracer as a slightly wider sweep over the forearm section.

Now I'm working out the naming convention for the arm chains—shoulder, elbow, hand joints labeled with L/R suffixes based on which side of the body they're on, so the pauldron, bracer, and other attachments can reference the correct joint by name.

For the shoulder joints, I need to position them symmetrically at the sides of the chest, parented to the chest bone. Then for the arm thickness profile, I'm varying the radius along the chain to give a believable biceps taper—thicker near the shoulder, bulging slightly at the bicep point, then narrowing toward the elbow and wrist.

For the sleeves, I'm adding a short rolled cloth cuff over the upper arm using a swept radius with flat caps, and thinking about bracers on the forearm with a darker leather/steel tone plus gold stud detailing along the sweep.

Placing the studs with a ring arrangement around the arm's dorsal point, facing outward with a matching radius to the bracer so small gold spheres sit embedded at each position.

Now I'm defining the leg chains next: hip, knee, ankle joints as a three-point chain parented to the hips, with contact points at the foot base, skipping a separate toe joint for simplicity and letting foot parts attach directly to the ankle bone.

I'm planning the pants in dark brown cloth, with boots built from tapering radius sweeps up the leg plus a thicker folded cuff band at the top in a wool tone, and considering a simple ellipsoid-style block for the foot shape itself.

Modeling the foot as a capsule tube running from heel to toe, wide and slightly flattened so it sits flush on the ground, then adding a steel toe cap as a shorter, slightly larger capsule layered over the front of the boot.

Now I'm sketching a flat dark sole box underneath, sized to touch the floor exactly, and wiring up the ankle point to connect leg and foot cleanly. For the torso I'm placing a brown pelvis ellipsoid between the legs for pants, and considering adding a leather pack or bedroll on the back to strengthen the dwarf blacksmith silhouette from behind.

I'm keeping the hammer and tongs holstered on the belt with a hip pouch and belt rag, plus a small leather satchel at the lower back. Then I'm scattering ginger chest-hair cards above the tunic's V-neck on the upper torso surface, and setting up beard card scatters on the beard ellipsoid with a downward-leaning flow.

Now I'm cataloging the texture set: an eye decal, a hair strand card gradient from dark root to light tip, a clan crest (anvil and hammer on shield) for apron and shoulder disc, a glowing rune strip for the anvil, a goggle lens plane, an ember spark card, and a stitched leather strap texture I'll likely skip.

I'm deciding to reuse the circular CREST medallion for the pauldron disc, belt buckle, and apron decal rather than make separate textures, skipping extra icons for the tunic collar and keeping the list lean.

For the forearm, I'm placing a blue-ink rune band decal using the sweep's point-and-normal frame to orient it correctly on the arm surface. Tallying textures now: eye, strand, crest, rune, lens, spark, and tattoo, with maybe one more still to add.

Now I'm sketching the SVG eye shape — outlining the almond outline, adding a cream-toned eyeball fill, and setting up the iris circle with a cool blue or amber tone fitting for a dwarf's deep-set eyes.

Shaping the strand as a blade tapering to a point at top, wide at bottom where it roots into the card, with a gradient running dark ginger to bright. Then for the crest I'm designing a round medallion with a gold outer ring, blue inner field, and an anvil silhouette inside.

Still writing crest and rune glyph shapes...

For the lens, I'm planning a circular gradient from teal to deep blue with a white glint highlight, kept opaque and placed on a flat circle without extra glow.

For the spark, I'm designing a teardrop streak with a yellow core and orange edges, then scattering small glowing cards oriented with random upward-fanning directions from the impact point using frame-based placement so they catch the light from multiple angles.

Now I'm sketching the tattoo as a blue zigzag rune-chain with dotted accents.

Tallying textures, I land on seven or eight total between eye, strand, crest, rune, lens, spark, and tattoo, and I'm double-checking the glow constraint that targets need a single standard material rather than a painted one, since flat colors and texture-based parts handle that differently with cards returning mesh arrays. For the hot blade, I'm laying out four extrude segments transitioning from a cool tang color to a glowing orange-red near the tip.

Defining blade width profile...

Working out the blade placement at x=-0.32, computing the thickness direction via cross product to get a downward-centered extrusion, and checking the anvil top aligns with the blade's bottom edge at y=0.78. I'm confirming adjacent segments share edges cleanly without z-fighting, then moving to figure out the segment boundary coordinates.

I'm defining a piecewise-linear width function along the blade, widening at the shoulder then stepping down sharply into the tang (separate thin segment from 0.42 to 0.56). I'm assigning color bands to each segment from yellow-white near the tip to dark grey for the tang, and computing where the tongs grip the tang shoulder (around x=0.16) to figure out the tongs' hand target position.

Now I'm extending the tongs' jaw from the grip point J=(0.16,0.795,0.55) back through the hand to find where the handle ends, roughly 1.7x the J-to-C distance, landing near z=0.23, y=0.87 -- which looks like it might collide with the apron near the belly, so I need to check that.

Settling on a shorter 1.45x length so the tongs end at z≈0.275, clearing the apron front at ~0.245.

Now working out the left arm IK: shoulder at (0.31,0.99,0), target (0.22,0.84,0.36), with upper arm 0.24 and forearm 0.22 summing close to the actual distance of 0.41, so the elbow bend will be shallow but fine.

For the right arm, shoulder (-0.31,0.99,0) to target (-0.27,1.1,0.32), distance 0.34 versus the 0.46 arm length sum, meaning there's more room for elbow bend there.

Now computing the hammer's orientation: I'm normalizing the swing direction vector, placing the handle along it from -0.13 to +0.38 of the hand position, and setting the head's long axis perpendicular to that direction via a cross product so it tilts up-back — checking the dot product confirms it's perpendicular. This gives a mid-swing pose where the striking face angles down-forward toward the blade, which matches a dwarf swinging the hammer forward-down. I'm now sizing the hammer head's central body dimensions.

Designing the head as a cross-peen hammer: a boxy body with a flat striking face on one end and a tapered chisel-like peen spike on the other, oriented along the swing axis. I'm also considering adding glowing rune engravings on the side face of the head, positioned using the local X-axis of the box so they align with whichever face points closest to the creature's right side.

Adjusting rune plane orientation...

Now I'm figuring out bone assignments for the props: the hammer rides the right hand bone, tongs ride the left hand, and anvil/stump pieces attach to hips as the root since they're freestanding props not tied to a limb chain.

I'm checking the floor-level geometry next—making sure the stump base sinks to y=0, nothing clips below ground, and boot soles sit flush at zero so the whole figure reads as standing properly.

Now I'm setting up imports for the build: pulling in Three.js core, the builder utilities (frame, limb, catmull, paint, noise, etc.) from the agentic-3js-builder SDK, plus the metal and glow kits. I want to confirm noise, mix, and smoothstep are actually exported from the index before relying on them.

Since this is strict TypeScript with unused-variable checks enabled, I need to stay careful about only importing what I actually use. I'm setting up a type alias for the builder instance, a small vector helper, and side constants for left/right symmetry before diving into the main geometry code.

Now I'm defining the material palette: metals like gold, brass, bronze, steel, iron, and a darkened steel, plus a procedural blue paint that blends colors using noise and lighting based on surface normals.

I'm sketching out leather, apron, and clothing materials next — mottled browns for leather with soot darkening at the base, and mottled blue/brown fabrics for the tunic and pants using small-scale noise patterns.

For the beard, I'm designing a ginger color palette that mixes warm orange-red tones along a noise gradient, aiming for that bright Warcraft-style ginger look with darker undertones.

Now I'm starting the skeleton build function, defining the dwarf blacksmith builder and setting the hips as the root spine joint.

Building the spine chain with catmull-rom points for the torso, naming the joints spine1, spine2, and chest, each positioned progressively upward and slightly forward toward the chest.

Now I'm setting up the neck as a polyline chain from the chest to a point above, then adding separate head and jaw joints that attach to the neck, each with their own position and aim direction for later posing.

For the arms, I'm computing shoulder positions symmetrically from the chest width, then defining left/right target positions and bend offsets for each arm so the sweeps can follow natural-looking poses on both sides.

The three-point path should pass fine as a polyline with corner rounding at the elbow, and chain order needs the first joint on the correct side (x>0 for L, matching shoulder positions at ±0.3). Now I'm setting up the hip position and foot target for the legs.

Checking the leg limb distance (~0.439) fits within the max reach (0.53), so the knee bends forward naturally; I'm naming the chain joints hip/knee/ankle, parenting them to hips with role "leg" and defining ground contact points. Now I'm building the torso loft with a series of width/height cross-sections rising from the hips up through the chest.

Adding more torso stations, then considering the tunic coverage in blue cloth, checking the loft's front/back depth at the belly works out correctly, and adding a trapezius ellipsoid at the chest bone. I'm skipping separate pectoral detail since the tunic covers it, but noting the neck stays bare skin, and now thinking through how to shape the V-neck opening in the tunic to reveal some chest hair.

Writing collar torus code...

Adding brow ridges now, positioning small rotated ellipsoids on each side of the skull with a slight tilt to give an angry, asymmetric slope outward from center.

For eyebrows, I'm sweeping a bushy ginger strand along a curved path from inner to outer brow, using a polyline with tapered radius and round caps, bound to the head bone.

I'm finishing the eyebrow coordinates, then placing the eyes beneath the brow ridge checking they're not fully obscured, adding cheek ellipsoids for paint markings, and positioning the nose with small nostril bumps and a reddened tip.

I'm giving the nose a reddish skin tone, deciding how the mustache covers the mouth area, and adding a small dark ellipsoid for the mouth cavity plus a red lower lip on the jaw, then starting the ear ellipsoid dimensions.

Adding gold earring torus geometry and rotation, then sketching the mustache curve points that sweep outward and down to form the dwarf's big sideways mustache shape.

Working out the beard geometry, I need it to bulge forward as it falls from chin to chest, widening and projecting further in z the lower it goes before tapering back in near the torso.

I'm planning to rig it as a single rigid bone loft on the jaw joint and paint it ginger, with the beard overlapping the apron top and braids hanging from around chest height on either side.

Now I'm scattering individual strand cards across the beard loft's surface, tuning their size, lean, flow direction, and bend so they drape naturally and pick up the ginger coloring, and making sure each card inherits the jaw bone for rigging with roughly 70 strands total.

Then I'm working out the braid placement, tracing a path down from the beard side toward the torso front and belly, checking that the braid radius clears the apron thickness so it doesn't clip into the torso surface.

Since the path has no explicit bone, each braid segment will just attach to the nearest joint, likely the chest or spine—that works naturally. For the braid itself, I'll generate twelve ellipsoid links with alternating colors along the path.

I could treat each link as a bead with a rope-like appearance, so alternating colors read as a braid, and add gold torus rings at intervals rotated so their axis aligns with the tangent direction rather than the default Z axis. Then I'd use a path-walking function to place beads along the sampled points.

I'm planning a gold spike/tassel cap for the braid ends, estimating roughly 16 parts per braid across the beard and mustache braids (~32 total), keeping the full part count near 250. For hair, I'm placing ellipsoids at the back of the head, sideburns blending into the beard, and a ponytail braid path starting near the head's base.

Now I'm reusing the braid function for the back ponytail with adjusted path points matching the torso's back curvature, scattering extra hair cards there, and starting on the pauldron code that computes shoulder position and axis per side and references the arm's shoulder joint. Writing pauldron placement logic...

I decide to skip the lathe's built-in smoothing option since it risks corner-crossing errors, opting instead for a manually curved multi-point dome outline with flat-shaded segments for a faceted look.

Working out the three-lame arrangement...

Still fanning out the lames with increasing outward tilt per layer, keeping them blue with gold trim rings at the base using thin torus geometry oriented along each lame's axis, then starting on the top spike piece.

For the rivets, I need a helper function that computes points around a circle on an arbitrary axis using quaternion rotation to orient a local ring into the right direction, then merges those stud positions around the dome base.

Writing merge helper for studs...

Now I'm thinking about whether to add a crest medallion disc on the pauldron's lame side.

I'm adjusting the ray angle to properly hit the dome's outer slope near the rim, bumping elevation to around 35° and guarding against a null hit from the raycast. I'm also noting the pauldrons need to attach to the shoulder bone to move naturally with the arms.

Now I'm computing the apron's silhouette by sampling torso front-surface z-depth at several y-stations (chest, belly, etc.) and adding a small thickness margin at each point, building up the profile for a catmull-rom loft from chest to knee.

I'm weighing whether to rig the apron to the hips or the spine bone. For safety I'll go with a rigid attachment to the hips, even though that means the apron won't bend with the torso loft during animation—an acceptable tradeoff. I'm also second-guessing whether the loft section type supports a flattened box profile versus defaulting to a thin ellipse.

I'll keep the box section option anyway since unsupported parameters likely get ignored rather than erroring, and now I'm sketching out apron details—a tattered scalloped bottom edge, a crest decal, and a small leather pocket box positioned on the front using an extrude at the apron's front z-depth.

I'm placing the pocket trapezoid with scalloped edges centered on the apron front, then adding a few small rods sticking out as tool handles (tongs, rasp) in dark wood/brass tones.

Now I'm working on the neck strap: checking where the yoke ellipsoid surface sits relative to the shoulder to find a valid drape height, then setting up a surface drape between torso and yoke to lay the strap naturally over the shoulders.

I'll sweep the strap path with a small flat radius profile, but since the tube's orientation varies along the curve, I'll just go with a round cross-section for simplicity rather than trying to perfectly align flat sides with the surface normal.

For the belt, I'll loop it around the torso at hip height using the surface loop function, letting it default to world-up orientation. I need to check that the apron doesn't visually conflict with the belt since the apron sits further out along z and the belt is positioned at y=0.62.

Checking the belt dimensions against the apron width confirms good coverage at the sides with a small clean gap. I'm building the belt as a closed catmull curve with twelve points around an elliptical path, varying the tube radius slightly for a tapered look, which should avoid needing a separate loop seam. I still need to account for how the apron tucks under the belt near the top where their z-centers differ slightly by height.

Adding studs around the belt as a ring of rivets at offset angles, plus a hip pouch box hanging off the left side at belt height.

Placing the hammer head below the handle end, then adding a soot-stained rag hanging from the belt as a small cloth box. I'm also sketching a back satchel with a flap and a bedroll cylinder strapped across the top.

For the legs, I'm planning leather knee pads positioned slightly forward and up from each knee joint with a steel rim, following the bend of the leg's sweep chain. I'm now working out boot geometry along the ankle portion of that same leg chain.

Writing boot sweeps...

Checking the proportions, the full foot span of 0.36 feels too long for a dwarf's chunky boot, so I'm shortening it to heel at -0.02 and toe at 0.13, giving roughly 0.30 total — better scaled. I'm also confirming the ankle and leg-bottom heights line up with the boot tube, then sketching the toe cap as a short sweep between two points with tapered radius for a rounded steel-dark cap.

Adjusting the toe cap position slightly inward so it doesn't overshoot the boot's silhouette, and making sure its radius is just a touch larger than the boot's own toe radius so it sits naturally on top. I'm sizing a flat sole box to match the boot's width with a small margin, then starting to lay out a small gold buckle strap as a ring sweep on the boot.

Now I'm adding a horizontal strap torus around the ankle area in belt color with a gold buckle box positioned at the front where the torus curve meets the leg, then moving on to set up cuff bracers at the wrist before defining a helper function to build the hand/fist shape from bone joints.

Computing finger orientation axes...

Still placing hand geometry...

Now I'm figuring out the tongs' two rods, having them cross near a pivot point between the jaw and handle end, then simplifying to two straight bars with offset positions at the jaw and handle for a realistic crossing grip.

Reducing the separation to 0.02 keeps the bars within the finger capsule radius, so I'm adjusting the bar endpoints accordingly and adding small jaw tip pieces near the pivot for grip detail.

Now I realize the separation axis is wrong — since the blade lies along x, the tongs would need to approach from a different direction to grip the tang properly. I think I'll reconsider the blade's orientation or the tongs' approach angle to make the geometry make sense.

Checking the hand position against shoulder distance, I verify the arm length works with the elbow bending outward, placing the jaws near the tang end of the blade. I'm computing the vector from jaws to hand, finding it points mostly backward in z, meaning the tongs approach the tang from behind.

Now I'm trying different blade orientations, rotating it by yaw so the tang end sits toward the back-left and the tip points forward-right, then checking whether the reversed blade direction roughly matches the tongs' approach vector.

That's too long for the anvil's face though, diagonal placement would overhang the front edge. Maybe I should shorten the billet to a short blade blank, or instead have the tongs hold the tang from over the horn, with the hand extended laterally beyond it.

Actually that reach distance exceeds the arm's limit too, so I need a different pose entirely. Let me reconsider the whole stance: have the dwarf stand facing the anvil's face with the horn on his left (typical right-handed smith stance), and hold the billet across the face in his left hand while the hand sits just to the left of the tongs grip.

I'm checking the angle between the tongs' grip direction and the blade orientation—about 42° off, which is a bit awkward but tongs jaws are bent in reality so it should read fine visually. I'll just settle on the blade running roughly along the x-axis with a slight yaw rather than overengineering the geometry further.

Now I'm computing the tip position with a small yaw angle and checking it stays within the anvil's top box bounds—the z and x coordinates both come out borderline but acceptable. I'm adjusting the total length to 0.5 split between tang and blade to keep everything compressed within the earlier segment bounds.

Working out the orientation vectors for the blade extrusion, deriving the direction from tip to tang and the perpendicular width direction from the yaw angle, then cross-multiplying to get the thickness axis.
